newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Burns Philp settles Estate Mortgage dispute.
newsitem.headline: Burns Philp settles Estate Mortgage dispute.

text.p: Troubled Australian food group Burns, Philp & Co Ltd reached a settlement in the long-running Estate Mortgage dispute on Monday, agreeing a pay-out of around A$115 million (US$85 million).

News of the deal pushed Burns Philp's shares up eight cents to A$2.52 in early trade, their highest level in a year and two cents above the price at which New Zealand investor Graeme Hart recently took a 19.9-percent interest in the group.
The long-running dispute follows the 1990 collapse of the Estate Mortgage Trusts with debts of about A$600 million, wiping out the retirement savings of about 56,000 elderly investors.

Burns Philp subsidiary Burns Philp Trustee Co, the trustee for Estate Mortgage, was one of a number of a number of parties taken to the Victorian Supreme Court in February after attempts at mediation failed.
Burns Philp said it had agreed to pay Estate Mortgage, renamed Meridian Investment Trust under new trustees, A$90 million in cash and 12 million convertible notes at A$2.20 each.
Meridian, which is managed by Tyndall Australia Ltd -- 52 percent owned by Sir Ron Brierley's Guinness Peat Group -- said the settlement was worth a minimum A$116.4 million.
Burns Philp chairman Alan McGregor said he was pleased all claims against the company had been settled as it would allow the group to concentrate fully on its businesses.
"Estate Mortgage has taken up many hours of management time and the costs associated with mounting a complex legal case such as this are significant," McGregor said.
Burns Philp currently has its North American and European herb and spice businesses on the market after an unsuccessful attempt to become a global player.
The company is also looking for a new chief executive to replace Ian Clack, who announced he would step down in May.
Burns Philp sought a week's adjournment of the case on Monday and legal sources said it was likely an attempt would be made to reach an out-of-court settlement with other parties.
The court case alone is estimated to have cost up A$24 million during the past six months.
Meridian settled with Estate Mortgage's auditors Priestley & Morris in April, receiving a A$31 million payout.
Meridian trustee John Murphy said the case against remaining defendants, including legal firm Freehill Hollingdale & Page and professional indemnity insurers, would be pursued vigorously.
Units in the listed Meridian Investment Trust, which united and rationalised the old Estate Mortgage loan portfolio, rose 11 cents on the deal to A$1.58.
